sentences.text: The holotype specimen, which is the specific fossil the species is based on, consists of a very elongated cervical vertebra, likely the fifth one, measuring between 77 and 78 cm in length.
Known remains include fragmentary bones such as parts of the skull, lower jaw, a partial femur, a partial radius, a partial humerus, two phalanges, and several partial cervical vertebrae.
Arambourgiania possessed a much weaker neck than the giant predator Hatzegopteryx, indicated by its lithe, thin-walled vertebrae and fewer muscle attachments designed to support a robust head.
This animal was among the largest azhdarchids, comparable in size to Quetzalcoatlus, Hatzegopteryx, and possibly Cryodrakon.
Its bones were extremely hollow and lightly built, featuring specific adaptations for soaring flight.
Arambourgiania is part of the only pterosaur group for which trackways have been confidently assigned, showing that it walked with its limbs held directly underneath its body.
Based on the holotype, researchers extrapolated the total neck length of the animal to be about 3 meters.
In 1943, a railway worker discovered fossil fragments including an incomplete cervical vertebra measuring 60.96 cm during phosphate mining near Ruseifa, Jordan.
Paleontologist Camille Arambourg described the specimen as a new genus and species, Titanopteryx philadelphiae, in 1959.
The original holotype material, combined with plaster, was approximately 62 cm long but was sawed into three parts with the middle section now missing.
In 1999, Wendy Melton-Beeson discovered and T. Lynn Harrell Jr. collected a fragmentary azhdarchid cervical vertebra in Selmer, Tennessee.
In 2018, David Martill and Markus Moser described fragmentary azhdarchid specimens from the Bavarian State Collection in Munich.

While historically interpreted as soarers, some authors have suggested Arambourgiania could have performed flapping flight similar to swans and geese, though a 2024 study suggests it was a soarer based on adaptations in its humerus similar to those in vultures.
Researchers suggest that Arambourgiania likely did not have a piscivorous lifestyle similar to modern skim-feeders.
No azhdarchid fossils, including those of Arambourgiania, have been found in truly terrestrial strata.
Arambourgiania is classified as a member of the pterosaur family Azhdarchidae.
In 1984, Nessov assigned Arambourgiania, then known as Titanopteryx, to the subfamily Azhdarchinae within the family Pteranodontidae.
The genus Arambourgiania was formally described by Nesov et al. in 1987.
Arambourgiania lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the Maastrichtian age, inhabiting Jordan during this time approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.
During the Maastrichtian, the sites where Arambourgiania fossils were found in Jordan and Morocco were covered by the Tethys Sea.
Fragments of cervical vertebrae attributed to Arambourgiania have been found in Jordan and the United States.
In 1975, Douglas A. Lawson concluded that the holotype specimen was a cervical vertebra rather than a wing metacarpal, correcting an earlier interpretation.
A 2014 study suggests the endocasts referred to Arambourgiania by Lewy likely belong to birds due to their 3 cm length and bird-like structure.
Fossil remains from the United States and Morocco have been tentatively assigned to Arambourgiania, though this classification is not certain.

Estimates for the wingspan of Arambourgiania vary significantly; in the late 1990s, Frey and Martill estimated it between 11 and 13 meters, while a 2003 suggestion of 7 meters provided no rationale, leading Witton and Habib to debate whether the smaller figure was an underestimate and the larger one an overestimate, with a 2022 proposal of 8 to 9 meters suggesting it was smaller than Quetzalcoatlus northropi, and a 2024 study estimating it around 10 meters based on comparisons with the humerus of Quetzalcoatlus northropi.
